title: The Day I Stopped Arguing About Choreography vs Orchestration
partialText:
“The danger is that it’s very easy to make nicely decoupled systems with event notification, without realizing that you’re losing sight of that larger-scale flow, and thus set yourself up for trouble in future years.”
Martin Fowler, What do you mean by “Event-Driven?” (2017)

Let me say the quiet part out loud: more event-driven systems than anyone admits aren’t decoupled by design. They’re decoupled by avoidance.

Few teams actually sit in a room, weigh choreography against orchestration, and pick choreography on the merits. In my experience, the deciding factor is usually far more practical than architectural: nobody wants to build and own an orchestrator. And honestly, I get it. I’ve built the home-grown one: the tidy state machine that grows, release by release, into a God Service every request waits on. I’ve reached for Temporal when I got tired of maintaining my own. I know what orchestration costs. So when a team reaches for pure events instead, I don’t blame them.

But it usually goes the same way. The happy path ships, and it’s gorgeous: services react to events, nobody’s coupled to anybody, adding a consumer is free. Then the first real failure lands. Payment fails after inventory’s already reserved and the “thanks for your order” email is already gone. And the part nobody wanted to build, the compensation, the “who undoes what,” has no owner. It was never designed. It’s smeared across five services that each did their job perfectly.

The danger Fowler named up top has been chewed over a hundred times since, by Hohpe, by Chris Richardson, by every conference talk on the subject. I’m not here to relitigate it. I’ve stood in both camps long enough to be tired of the tribalism anyway. So instead of planting a flag in one, I tried to reconcile them. Which meant dropping the question everyone argues about, “choreography or orchestration?”, for a better one:

Where do we actually need coordination?

Once I looked, the answer was almost embarrassing:

  • The happy path needs almost none.
  • The failure path needs almost all of it.

That reconciliation is the whole article: choreograph the ordinary, orchestrate the exceptions. When you take the orchestrator off the happy path, four things lose their home:

  • Visibility: one place that knows where every process stands.
  • An explicit state machine: the flow written down, not implied.
  • Explicit compensation: a readable answer to “what do we undo?”
  • One place to reason about the process as a whole.

The rest of this is about giving those four a home again, without putting a coordinator back on the critical path. One admission up front, so you read the rest fairly: in most systems I’d still reach for a real workflow engine. This is what I found when I asked what the leaner, reconciled version would even look like.

The happy path was never the hard part

Start with pure choreography, because on the nominal path it genuinely shines.

OrderCreated ──▶ Payment ──▶ PaymentSucceeded ──▶ Shipping ──▶ Shipped

Each service subscribes to the events it cares about, does its work, and publishes what happened. Order doesn't know Payment exists. Payment doesn't know about Shipping. Adding a consumer is free:

OrderCreated ──┬──▶ Fraud check
               ├──▶ Analytics
               └──▶ Recommendations

No producer changes. Nobody redeploys. With durable queues, retries, and idempotent handlers, the system just converges. This is choreography at its best, and it’s a real best: low coupling, easy extension, natural resilience.

For the path where everything goes right, it’s hard to beat. The trouble is that the path where everything goes right is the part you were never worried about.

Then the happy path ends

Let the flow grow the way real flows do:

OrderCreated
   ├─▶ PaymentRequested
   ├─▶ InventoryReserved
   ├─▶ FraudChecked
   ├─▶ CustomerNotified
   └─▶ ShippingStarted

Now inject reality. Payment fails, but inventory is already reserved, the customer already got a “thanks for your order” email, and shipping has begun pulling the item. Five services each did exactly their job. The system as a whole is now in a state no one designed and no one owns.

So: who decides what to undo?

In pure choreography, the answer isn’t quite “nobody.” In practice you wire up reactions: Inventory listens for PaymentFailed, Notification listens for OrderCancelled. The problem isn't that no one reacts. It's that responsibility for the whole is now distributed, implicit, and harder to reason about with every service you add. No single participant holds the process. It's smeared across all of them. Compensations, timeouts, stuck flows, partial failures: the entire category of "it didn't go as planned" has no home you can point at.

That’s the real weakness, and it’s worth saying plainly: choreography is excellent at making things happen, and terrible at owning what happens next. The failure itself is rarely hidden. PaymentFailed fires an event; a poisoned message lands in a dead-letter queue; the logs have it. What's missing is an owner. That DLQ entry just sits there, and unwinding the rest of the order, releasing the inventory, cancelling, refunding, telling the customer, is nobody's job in particular. Every service handled its own piece correctly. No one is responsible for the whole. An unhandled dead-letter queue isn't a rare edge case, and it isn't recovery. It's just where ownership goes to die.

Orchestration fixes that, and files the bill in the wrong place

The classic answer is to give the process an owner.

Order Workflow
  1. Create order
  2. Reserve inventory
  3. Charge payment
  4. Notify customer
  5. Complete

Now one component knows where you are, what’s next, and what to do when a step fails. Visibility is excellent. Compensation is explicit. You can read the workflow top to bottom.

But look at what you paid. Every step now routes through the orchestrator. It couples to the shape of the workflow: add a step, touch the orchestrator. It drifts toward being a God Service that knows everything and that everything waits on. And here’s the part that actually matters:

You pay that coupling on every single request, including the overwhelming majority that would have sailed through choreography untouched. You put a coordinator on the critical path to solve a problem that shows up on a small fraction of executions.

The failure handling is worth having. Putting a coordinator on the critical path of every request to get it, including the overwhelming majority that never needed it, is the mistake.

Coordinate where the coordination actually is

We already know the shape: the happy path needs almost no coordination, the failure path needs almost all of it. So don’t put the coordinator on the path that doesn’t need one. Keep the happy path choreographed: decoupled, event-driven, autonomous. Then add a component that sits off to the side, watches the event stream, and stays completely out of the way until the flow leaves the rails.

Order ─────▶ event ─┐
Payment ───▶ event ─┼──▶  (the event stream)
Shipping ──▶ event ─┘
                         │  observes
                         ▼
                  Process Manager
                         │  acts only on deviation
                         ▼
              compensate · retry · escalate

On the nominal path, the process manager is passive. It reads events, keeps its picture of each flow current, and emits nothing: no commands, no interference. The moment something fails (a failure event, a message rotting in a dead-letter queue), it acts: triggers compensations, drives a retry policy, or escalates to a human.

Here’s the distinction that makes it work: business services own their own step. The process manager owns the flow between them. Every other participant sees only its own slice, reacts, and moves on. The process manager is the one component that holds the process as a whole, and so the only one that can decide what the whole should do when a step fails.

Normal:                     Deviated:
  OrderCreated                OrderCreated
  PaymentSucceeded            PaymentFailedRetryable
  OrderCompleted              retry ×3 → timeout
  → process mgr idle          → process mgr: compensate, cancel, page an operator

I’m not trying to orchestrate success. Success already has a perfectly good coordination mechanism: events. The proposal was never to replace choreography. It’s to stop asking it to solve the one problem it was never built to solve. I’m orchestrating recovery, and nothing else.

Take compensation, the messiest of the four. In pure choreography it scatters across everyone:

PaymentFailed
   ├─▶ Inventory listens    → release stock
   ├─▶ Order listens        → cancel the order
   └─▶ Notification listens → tell the customer

To understand what happens when a payment fails, you reconstruct it in your head from four separate subscriptions. With a process manager, the same recovery is one readable sequence:

PaymentFailed ──▶ Process Manager
                    ├─▶ CompensateInventory
                    ├─▶ CancelOrder
                    └─▶ NotifyCustomer

Even someone who prefers choreography can admit the second one is easier to read, and easier to get right. That’s one of the four benefits back, and the happy path never moved.

And no, this isn’t a new pattern. It has several old names, and I’ll get to them in a minute. The idea worth keeping is the placement, not the label.

Recovery belongs to the workflow, not the service

There’s a deeper point under that readability win, and it’s the part that actually convinced me.

The process manager is not holding a global table of PaymentFailedFinal → RefundPayment. That would be brittle, enormous, and exactly the God Service everyone rightly fears. It owns one workflow at a time. In Checkout, a final payment failure means: release the stock, cancel the order, maybe issue a credit note instead of a cash refund. In Subscription Renewal, the same event means almost the opposite: keep the subscription alive through a grace period, send a reminder, cancel nothing yet. Same event, same Payment service, completely different recovery. The recovery was never a property of the payment. It was a property of the process.

Which is a principle worth putting on the wall:

Services own business capabilities. Workflows own business intent. Recovery belongs to intent, not to capability.

The Payment service knows how to authorize, capture, and refund. It has no idea whether, in this business context, a refund is even the right move, or whether to wait, retry, or issue credit instead. That was never Payment’s call. It belongs to the workflow.

And here’s the misread to head off, because it’s the one that turns people against the idea: I’m not moving business logic into the process manager. Payment still owns how to refund. The process manager owns exactly one new thing, the policy that only exists once a process has left its expected path: given that this checkout deviated here, if, when, and why to compensate. Never how. That single, narrow responsibility is the whole reason this doesn’t collapse into a God Service. It centralizes the business reasoning that only appears off the happy path, and nothing else.

This has a name: several, actually

None of this is new, and an experienced reader is already typing that in the comments. What I’ve built is a Process Manager in Gregor Hohpe’s sense: observe events, track state, issue commands when a decision is needed. With one deliberate twist. The textbook process manager actively drives the workflow from step to step; this one stays passive while the happy path runs itself, and only picks up the baton when a step fails. Which is exactly where the supervision tree sits in Erlang and Akka: the workers work, and something off to the side stays quiet until one of them fails. It’s also the recovery half of the Saga conversation.

Call it a Process Manager, a saga coordinator, whatever your stack already calls it. You could build it on Temporal, on a home-grown state machine, or on another engine entirely. The label and the implementation were never the point. The point is one sentence, and if I had to throw the rest of this away, I’d keep it:

Workflow execution and workflow reasoning don’t have to live in the same component.

Execution, the doing, stays choreographed, spread across autonomous services. Reasoning, what should have happened and what to do when it didn’t, gets exactly one home, off the critical path. Most orchestration fuses the two onto the happy path. Pulling them apart is the whole move.

What the process manager actually needs

Two things, and both come with a catch worth being honest about.

It needs a view. A process manager is only as good as the view it reasons from. The services shouldn’t expose their internals, so you build a projection from their events: an eventually consistent read model of where each process stands.

{
  "orderId": "123",
  "orderStatus": "CREATED",
  "paymentStatus": "FAILED_RETRYABLE",
  "retryCount": 3,
  "nextAction": "CANCEL"
}

That projection is your observability surface, your decision input, and your entry point for human intervention. Useful, and dangerous for the same reason: it lags. A process manager that reads payment failed and fires CANCEL can kill an order a late retry just completed. So the discipline is fixed: compensate idempotently, tolerate a stale view, reconcile rather than assume, and guard the executing services with optimistic locking so a stale CANCEL loses to a PaymentSucceeded that landed a second late. (Publish through a transactional outbox and the projection stops missing events, too.) An eventually consistent projection is exactly the kind of guarantee that isn't what it looks like: the assumption you inherit without noticing.

It needs to know the shape of the flow. To unwind a broken process correctly, the process manager has to know what the process was: which steps ran, in what order, and what compensates what. That model is real, and it has to live somewhere. Which is the honest catch: the workflow knowledge doesn’t vanish. It moves, out of an active orchestrator on the critical path and into a passive monitor beside it.

Be honest about that trade: you still have one place that knows the whole flow. The win isn’t that the knowledge disappeared. It’s that the thing holding it no longer sits between your services and no longer slows down the 99% of executions that were always going to be fine.

The knowledge doesn’t vanish. It just moves off the critical path.

Put together, the whole thing fits on one picture:

Happy path — choreographed, autonomous:
  Order ──▶ Payment ──▶ Shipping ──▶ ...
     │         │          │
     └──────── events ─────┘
                 │  observes everything
                 ▼
         Workflow Projection      (state of every in-flight process)
                 │  anomalies · timeouts
                 ▼
        Process Manager
                 │  acts only on deviation
                 ▼
         compensate · retry · escalate

The failure path is coupled, on purpose

One more thing not to oversell. When the process manager issues compensate payment, it is now coupled to Payment. It sends commands. It knows names.

You do get a dial here, if the coupling bothers you. The process manager can issue a direct command (CompensateInventory), or publish a high-level intent (OrderCancellationRequested) and let the services react to it the way they react to anything else. The first buys control and a single readable recovery sequence. The second buys back autonomy, at the cost of the one-place readability you came for. On the failure path I usually want the control, but it's a choice you make per workflow, not a property of the pattern.

The decoupling you preserved lives entirely on the happy path. The failure path deliberately trades autonomy for control, because control is precisely what you want when things are going wrong. That’s not a leak in the design; it’s the design. Just don’t stand up and claim the whole system is decoupled. Half of it is, on purpose, and the other half is coupled, on purpose.

When you shouldn’t do this

This is a specific shape, not a default. Skip it when:

  • The complexity is in the happy path itself. If your nominal flow has real sequencing, approval gates, or human-in-the-loop steps, a genuine orchestrator (or a workflow engine like Temporal) is simpler. Own the flow outright and stop pretending it’s choreographable.
  • The flow is short. Two steps and a retry don’t need a process manager. You need a queue.
  • You can’t stomach two coordination models. Choreography plus a process manager means two mental models in one system. That’s a real tax on everyone who reads the code later. Only pay it when the happy path is genuinely simple and the failure handling is genuinely gnarly, which, to be fair, is the exact shape of a lot of event-driven systems.

And the question you’ll get asked in every review: why not just Temporal? It’s the right question, and most of the time it has the boring answer: just use Temporal. A workflow engine hands you orchestration, durability, and visibility out of the box. And, above all, a workflow that is defined. Written down. Authoritative. You don’t infer where a process is; you ask the engine and it knows.

The hybrid can’t quite promise that, and it’s worth being honest about the gap. In Temporal, the workflow is the source of truth: reality is whatever the workflow says it is. In this hybrid, the event log is the source of truth, and the workflow is a projection, reconstructed from events and from what you believe the flow is supposed to be. That’s an inferred workflow, not a defined one. For monitoring, for auditing, for answering “where is this process,” a defined workflow beats an inferred one every time. (An inferred workflow is a pile of assumptions about what should happen, and you already know how that story ends.)

So no, I wouldn’t reach for this by default. In most systems I’d want the real engine: precisely for the monitoring, for a flow that’s actually defined instead of imagined, and for one place to manage behavior and compensation. The hybrid earns its keep only when happy-path autonomy is genuinely worth giving those up. Knowing when that’s true is the actual skill.

Workflow knowledge never disappears

I used to frame it as a fight: choreography versus orchestration, pick your tribe. That framing is the actual mistake. So I stopped trying to win the argument and tried to reconcile it. I didn’t escape orchestration. I stopped paying for it on the 99% of executions that never needed it, and put it exactly where it earns its keep: off the happy path, on the failures.

Choreography doesn’t eliminate coordination. It only hides where it happens, and waits for the first failure to remind you it was load-bearing all along.

And to be clear about what this is not: it isn’t a claim that orchestration beats choreography. The claim is narrower, and harder to dodge. In any non-trivial system, workflow knowledge ends up living somewhere: in Temporal, in a process manager, in a pile of event handlers, or in the heads of the three people who remember how it works. That somewhere is a design decision. Pretending it doesn’t exist is also a decision, just a worse one.

So the real question was never “should we orchestrate or choreograph?” It was always: where does workflow knowledge live, and did you choose that, or did production choose it for you?

Workflow knowledge never disappears. You don’t get to delete it. You only get to decide where it lives.

title: How We Built an MCP Server in Kotlin — Keeping Stdio Clean for JSON-RPC
partialText:
Kotlin · MCP · Developer Tools

I didn’t want to learn a new runtime to ship a tool for an AI agent.

I’m a Kotlin engineer. Coroutines, @Serializable data classes, Gradle modules, fat JARs — that's the stack I think in. When agents started showing up in editors and asking for tools, my first instinct wasn't to reach for Node or Python. It was to check whether Kotlin could close the loop. So I built gradle-opt-mcp — a server that gives Claude direct access to your Gradle build: dependency graphs, cache health, build scans, test summaries, all without pasting logs by hand.

The official Kotlin MCP SDK is real, actively maintained, and idiomatic. The stdio transport that Cursor, Claude Desktop, and Claude Code all use maps cleanly to a main function and a suspend-friendly server. Your @Serializable data classes become tool schemas. Your coroutines become the handler model. The fat JAR you already know how to build becomes the process the editor spawns.

One Android instinct killed my first session before a single tool call completed — and I didn’t know I had it until it broke.

stdout is the JSON-RPC socket. Every byte you write to it is protocol.

That’s the only new rule. Everything else is Kotlin you already know.

What the Process Actually Looks Like

Forget Ktor-on-a-port for a minute.

On the stdio transport, the MCP client owns your process entirely. Cursor, Claude Desktop, or Claude Code runs java -jar your-server.jar. Your main starts. Stdin becomes the incoming socket. Stdout becomes the outgoing socket. The parent process holds both ends of the pipe.

The handshake is deliberately boring. The client sends initialize. You respond with your server name, version, and declared capabilities. The client confirms with notifications/initialized. Then tools/list arrives, you answer with your catalog, and from there it's a stream of tools/call frames until stdin closes.

When stdin closes, you exit. Hang a thread and the editor is stuck with a process that can’t answer calls and won’t die.

That’s the entire runtime shape: one process tied to one editor session, with stdin and stdout as the only socket. The moment that picture is clear, the stdout rule stops feeling like a constraint. The wire was never yours to use.

The Instinct That Kills the Session

Kotlin engineers log to stdout. Not consciously — it’s just what println does, and on Android, Logback routes everything to logcat where it belongs and nothing breaks.

On stdio transport, it breaks immediately.

Ten minutes into my work, Cursor completely froze with no error message. When I ran the JAR manually and piped in an initialize frame, the response died mid-parse. It turns out a single line of Logback startup noise right before the opening { corrupted the frame format.

The fix is three lines. But the order matters more than the lines themselves.

You need to capture the real stdout before anything else in the process touches it. Before Logback initializes, before a single coroutine launches — before the JVM has any reason to touch stdout. Then redirect System.out to stderr — so every library that "prints normally" lands somewhere the protocol will never read. Then hand your saved reference to the transport.

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val mcpOutput = System.out      // capture the wire first
    System.setOut(System.err)       // redirect everything else to stderr
    val transport = StdioServerTransport(
        input = System.`in`.asSource().buffered(),
        output = mcpOutput.asSink().buffered()
    )
    // build server, register tools, createSession(transport)
}

Flip the order and you save a reference to stderr, not stdout. You protect the stream you poisoned.

After this swap, System.out is a controlled lie — any library that logs "normally" ends up on stderr, where the MCP client ignores it for framing. The actual wire is mcpOutput, handed directly to StdioServerTransport. They never cross.

The server shell — and why it should stay boring

With stdout safe, main has one job: wire the protocol skeleton and stay out of the way. If main knows how to parse a business error, it has already gotten too fat.

You construct a Server, declare your capabilities, attach the transport, then hand control to a list of registrars that build the actual tool catalog. Domain logic doesn't belong in this file.

val server = Server(
    serverInfo = Implementation(name = "my-kotlin-mcp", version = "1.0.0"),
    options = ServerOptions(
        capabilities = ServerCapabilities(
            tools = ServerCapabilities.Tools(listChanged = true)
        )
    )
)
registrars.forEach { it.register(server) }

ServerCapabilities.Tools is what tells the client you have tools to list. Without it, tools/list gets an empty handshake and the agent stops asking.

Each registrar calls server.addTool(...) with a name, description, schema, and a suspend handler. We hide that behind one interface so main stays a loop.

interface McpToolsRegistrar {
    fun register(server: Server)
}

Android engineers already think this way. The shell is the Activity. Registrars are the use cases. Real logic lives another layer down. The SDK shell just gives you one more place to practice the same discipline you already apply everywhere else.

Coroutines Close the Loop Cleanly

Because MCP tool handlers are suspend functions running within the SDK’s coroutine scope, you can invoke your existing suspend domain logic directly. There’s no need for callback adapters, thread pool management, or reactive wrappers.

The suspend model you use for ViewModel calls, repository fetches, and database queries in Android is the same model you use to answer a tools/call from Cursor. The mental context switch is zero.

server.addTool(
    name = "gradle_health",
    description = "Reports project health — modules, versions, structure.",
    inputSchema = toolSchema
) { args ->
    val projectDir = args[projectDirKey]?.jsonPrimitive?.content
        ?: return@addTool CallToolResult(
            content = listOf(TextContent("projectDir is required")),
            isError = true
        )
    val result = gradleHealthAnalyzer.analyze(projectDir)  // existing suspend fun
    CallToolResult(content = listOf(TextContent(result.toSummary())))
}

gradleHealthAnalyzer.analyze is the same suspend function used in a ViewModel. You called it directly, without rewriting or wrapping a single line.

That’s what stack closure feels like — not theoretical compatibility, but actually calling your own code without touching it.

Serializable Data Classes Become Your Tool Contracts

The other place the stack closes is payloads.

Agents don’t read your README mid-call. What you return from a tool handler is the contract — the model acts on it, or fails to, based entirely on what you gave it. String-glued JSON ages badly. One renamed field and the agent starts hallucinating the answer it expected.

We model tool inputs and outputs as @Serializable data classes, the same way we model API responses in Android. The class is the contract. The string projection into TextContent is the display.

@Serializable
data class AnalysisResult(
    val projectDir: String,
    val summary: String,
    val findings: List<String>,
    val truncated: Boolean,
    val failureReason: String? = null
)

truncated: true tells the model the list is incomplete. A bare "…" in prose means the agent reports it saw everything when it didn't. failureReason distinguishes "scan failed" from "filter matched nothing" from "no reports yet" — three different states that look identical if you return 0 findings for all of them.

Same instinct as a clean Android API: one well-typed return value instead of “here’s a file, go parse it.”

Lifecycle — the Process Shape That Matches What You Already Know

On Android, Application lives as long as the OS allows. The process lifetime is long, indeterminate, and managed externally. On stdio MCP, the process lifetime is exactly one editor session. Stdin closes, you exit.

The implementation is clean coroutines. We park on a CompletableDeferred until server.onClose fires, and wrap createSession in runCatching so a hard transport close doesn't spray an uncaught exception across stderr after the work is done.

val done = CompletableDeferred<Unit>()
server.onClose { done.complete(Unit) }
runCatching {
    server.createSession(transport)
}
done.await()

runBlocking around main is sufficient. You're not managing a long-lived process with background jobs. You're a short-lived RPC worker. The scope is the session. When the session ends, you end.

If it works in the IDE and fails inside Cursor, check lifecycle first. A hung Job and a stdout-sharing bug look identical from the outside: the client gets no response and gives you nothing to debug.

Prove It on the Wire, Not in a Unit Test

Unit tests don’t catch the stdout bug. I know because I had them.

You prove it with a real stdio test. Ship the fat JAR, pipe in JSON-RPC frames, and separate stdout (protocol) from stderr (logs). If Logback leaks a single line to stdout before the initial {, the protocol breaks—and your only warning will be silent failure in the editor.

Minimum sequence to trust your boot path:

  1. initialize (request id 1)
  2. notifications/initialized
  3. tools/call against a tool you trust (request id 3)

If step 3 returns a framed result and stderr stayed clean, the server is sound. Then kill the PID — don't leave a background JAR holding filesystem locks.

Android engineers already know this class of lie. The green unit test and the device are different worlds. The IDE and the hosted subprocess are the same gap. Trust the wire.

The Stack Closes. One Habit Changes.

The stack didn’t change. Just one rule at the top of main.

The fat JAR we already know how to build is the process Cursor spawns. The suspend functions we already write are the tool handlers. The @Serializable data classes we already use are the tool contracts. The CompletableDeferred pattern we already reach for is the session lifecycle.

Every piece was already there. The only thing that changed was one rule, applied once, at the top of main: capture the wire before anything else can touch it.

Agents are going to keep asking for tools. If you already write Kotlin, you already have the whole stack. You just have to unlearn the one habit that assumes stdout is yours.

GitHub - JosephSanjaya/gradle-opt-mcp: Give Claude eyes on your Gradle build via MCP - dependency graphs, build scans, cache health, and test summaries, no more pasting logs.

gradle-opt-mcp is the working reference — 14 tools, fat JAR, stdio transport, all of it in production Kotlin. Download a release or clone it if you want to see every pattern from this article running against a real Gradle project.
